question: What did the Iraq Survey Group conclude about Iraq's weapons of mass destruction after the 2003 invasion?
facts: The Iraq Survey Group's final report, known as the Duelfer Report, was released in 2004.
The Iraq Survey Group found that Iraq had no stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction at the time of the 2003 invasion.
The report concluded that Iraq had destroyed its chemical weapons stockpile in 1991, after the Gulf War.
The report found that Iraq's nuclear weapons program had ended in 1991 and had not been restarted.
The report judged that Saddam Hussein wanted to rebuild weapons programs once sanctions were lifted.

question: What did Colin Powell tell the UN Security Council about Iraq in February 2003, and how did his claims hold up?
facts: On 5 February 2003, US Secretary of State Colin Powell presented the US case against Iraq to the UN Security Council.
Powell claimed that Iraq had mobile biological weapons laboratories.
The mobile-laboratory claim relied heavily on an Iraqi defector code-named "Curveball".
Curveball's information was later judged to be fabricated.
No stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction were found in Iraq after the invasion.
Powell later described the speech as a "blot" on his record.

question: What did the US Senate Intelligence Committee find in 2004 about prewar intelligence on Iraq?
facts: In July 2004 the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence released a report on prewar intelligence assessments about Iraq.
The committee found that most major judgments in the October 2002 National Intelligence Estimate on Iraq were overstated or not supported by the underlying intelligence.
The committee attributed many of the errors to "groupthink" in the intelligence community.
The committee found that the claim that Iraq was reconstituting its nuclear program was not supported by the intelligence.

question: What was the claim that Iraq sought uranium from Niger, and what happened to it?
facts: In his January 2003 State of the Union address, President George W. Bush said the British government had learned that Saddam Hussein recently sought significant quantities of uranium from Africa.
The claim was tied to documents purporting to show Iraq trying to buy uranium yellowcake from Niger.
In March 2003 the International Atomic Energy Agency concluded that the Niger documents were forgeries.
Former ambassador Joseph Wilson travelled to Niger in 2002 for the CIA and reported that the purchase was very unlikely.
In July 2003 the White House acknowledged that the uranium sentence should not have been included in the speech.

question: What happened at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq in 2003 and 2004?
facts: US military personnel abused Iraqi detainees held at Abu Ghraib prison near Baghdad.
Photographs of the abuse became public in April 2004 through CBS's 60 Minutes II and The New Yorker.
The abuse included forced nudity, stress positions, sexual humiliation, and the use of dogs to intimidate detainees.
An Army investigation led by Major General Antonio Taguba described "sadistic, blatant, and wanton criminal abuses".
Specialist Charles Graner was convicted at court-martial and sentenced to ten years in prison.
Private First Class Lynndie England was convicted at court-martial for her role in the abuse.

question: Which official investigations examined the Abu Ghraib abuses, and what did they conclude about responsibility?
facts: Major General Antonio Taguba led an Army investigation into the military police at Abu Ghraib, completed in 2004.
The Fay-Jones investigation found that military intelligence personnel were also involved in the abuse.
The Schlesinger panel concluded that leadership failures at higher levels contributed to the abuse.
Brigadier General Janis Karpinski, who commanded the military police brigade running the prison, was demoted to colonel.
No senior officer above Karpinski was criminally charged over the abuse.

question: What did Edward Snowden reveal in 2013 about the NSA's collection of Americans' phone records?
facts: In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden showed that the NSA was collecting the telephone records of millions of Americans in bulk.
The first story, published by The Guardian, described a secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order requiring Verizon to hand over call records.
The bulk phone-records program operated under Section 215 of the USA PATRIOT Act.
The records collected were metadata such as phone numbers, call times and durations, not the content of calls.
Snowden was a contractor working for the NSA through Booz Allen Hamilton.

question: What was the NSA's PRISM program?
facts: PRISM was an NSA program disclosed in June 2013 from documents leaked by Edward Snowden.
Under PRISM the NSA obtained internet communications from major US technology companies including Microsoft, Google, Yahoo, Facebook and Apple.
PRISM operated under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, added by the FISA Amendments Act of 2008.
PRISM targeted non-US persons reasonably believed to be outside the United States, but communications of Americans could be collected incidentally.

question: How did US courts and Congress respond to the NSA's bulk collection of phone records?
facts: In May 2015 the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled in ACLU v. Clapper that the bulk phone-records program exceeded what Section 215 authorized.
Congress passed the USA FREEDOM Act in June 2015.
The USA FREEDOM Act ended the NSA's bulk collection of phone records, leaving the records with phone companies to be queried case by case.
In 2020 the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, in United States v. Moalin, found that the phone-records program was likely unlawful.

question: What did Director of National Intelligence James Clapper tell the Senate in March 2013 about NSA data collection on Americans?
facts: In March 2013 Senator Ron Wyden asked James Clapper whether the NSA collects any type of data at all on millions or hundreds of millions of Americans.
Clapper answered "No, sir" and added "not wittingly".
Documents leaked by Edward Snowden in June 2013 showed that the NSA was collecting phone metadata on millions of Americans.
Clapper later said his answer had been the "least untruthful" one he could give.

question: What happened in the US drone strike in Kabul on 29 August 2021?
facts: A US drone strike in Kabul on 29 August 2021 killed ten civilians, including seven children.
The strike targeted a car driven by aid worker Zemari Ahmadi, whom the US military wrongly believed to be an ISIS-K threat.
Zemari Ahmadi worked for the US-based aid group Nutrition and Education International.
US military leaders initially described it as a "righteous strike".
In September 2021 the Pentagon acknowledged the strike was a "tragic mistake" that killed civilians.
No US service members were disciplined for the strike.

question: How many civilians have been killed by US drone strikes in Pakistan, according to the US government and independent monitors?
facts: The United States conducted hundreds of drone strikes in Pakistan's tribal areas, mostly between 2004 and 2018.
Independent monitors such as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the New America Foundation tracked US drone strikes using media and field reports.
The Bureau of Investigative Journalism estimated that several hundred civilians were killed in US drone strikes in Pakistan.
In July 2016 the US Director of National Intelligence estimated that 64 to 116 non-combatants were killed in US strikes outside areas of active hostilities between 2009 and 2015.
The US government's civilian death estimates were far lower than those of independent monitors.

question: Who was Anwar al-Awlaki and how did he die?
facts: Anwar al-Awlaki was a US-born citizen and cleric linked to al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula.
Anwar al-Awlaki was killed by a US drone strike in Yemen in September 2011.
He was killed without being charged or tried in court.
A Justice Department Office of Legal Counsel memo provided the legal justification for targeting him.
His 16-year-old son Abdulrahman al-Awlaki, also a US citizen, was killed in a separate US strike in Yemen in October 2011.

question: What happened in the US-led coalition airstrike in the Mosul al-Jadida neighbourhood of Mosul on 17 March 2017?
facts: On 17 March 2017 a US airstrike hit a building in the Mosul al-Jadida neighbourhood of west Mosul during the battle against ISIS.
A US military investigation concluded that 105 civilians were killed in the building.
The US investigation said the strike set off explosives that ISIS fighters had placed in the building.
It was one of the deadliest incidents for civilians in the US-led air campaign against ISIS.

question: What was the CIA's Project MKUltra?
facts: MKUltra was a CIA program begun in 1953 under Director Allen Dulles.
MKUltra experimented on human subjects with drugs such as LSD, sometimes without their knowledge or consent.
The chemist Sidney Gottlieb led the program.
In 1973 CIA Director Richard Helms ordered most MKUltra records destroyed.
The program became public through the Rockefeller Commission and Church Committee investigations in the mid-1970s.
About 20,000 surviving financial documents were found in 1977 and discussed at Senate hearings that year.
Army scientist Frank Olson died in 1953 after being secretly given LSD in a CIA experiment.

question: What was the Tuskegee syphilis study?
facts: The US Public Health Service ran the study from 1932 to 1972 in Macon County, Alabama.
The study enrolled about 600 Black men, about 400 of whom had syphilis.
The men were not told they had syphilis and were not given informed consent.
The men were not treated with penicillin even after it became the standard cure in the 1940s.
The study was exposed in 1972 by Associated Press reporter Jean Heller, based on information from whistleblower Peter Buxtun.
President Bill Clinton formally apologized for the study in 1997.
The scandal led to the National Research Act of 1974 and new rules for research on human subjects.

question: What was the FBI's COINTELPRO program?
facts: COINTELPRO was a series of covert FBI programs run from 1956 to 1971.
COINTELPRO targeted domestic political groups, including the Communist Party, civil rights organizations, Black nationalist groups, and the New Left.
Its methods included infiltration, anonymous letters, planted media stories, and efforts to provoke conflict within groups.
COINTELPRO was exposed after activists broke into an FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania, in March 1971 and leaked the files.
In 1964 the FBI sent Martin Luther King Jr. an anonymous letter that has been widely read as urging him to kill himself.
The Senate's Church Committee investigated COINTELPRO in 1975 and 1976 and condemned its abuses.

question: How was Black Panther leader Fred Hampton killed?
facts: Fred Hampton, chairman of the Illinois Black Panther Party, was killed on 4 December 1969 in a pre-dawn police raid on his Chicago apartment.
The raid was carried out by officers attached to the Cook County State's Attorney's office.
FBI informant William O'Neal had given the FBI a floor plan of the apartment before the raid.
Panther member Mark Clark was also killed in the raid.
In 1982 the federal, county and city governments agreed to pay 1.85 million dollars to settle a civil suit by survivors and families.

question: What happened in the Gulf of Tonkin incident of August 1964?
facts: On 2 August 1964 the destroyer USS Maddox exchanged fire with North Vietnamese torpedo boats in the Gulf of Tonkin.
A second attack reported on 4 August 1964 most likely never happened.
Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution on 7 August 1964, authorizing President Johnson to use military force in Southeast Asia.
Only two senators, Wayne Morse and Ernest Gruening, voted against the resolution.
A declassified NSA history released in 2005 concluded that no attack took place on 4 August and that signals intelligence had been mishandled.

question: What is the Guantanamo Bay detention camp, and what has the Supreme Court said about it?
facts: The detention camp opened in January 2002 at the US naval base at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.
About 780 men have been held there.
Most detainees held at Guantanamo were never charged with a crime.
In Rasul v. Bush (2004) the Supreme Court ruled that US courts could hear habeas corpus petitions from Guantanamo detainees.
In Boumediene v. Bush (2008) the Supreme Court ruled that detainees have a constitutional right to habeas corpus.
President Obama ordered the camp closed in January 2009, but it remained open.

question: What did US officials conclude about the treatment of Guantanamo detainee Mohammed al-Qahtani?
facts: Mohammed al-Qahtani was suspected of being an intended hijacker in the 11 September 2001 attacks.
He was interrogated at Guantanamo in 2002 and 2003 with methods including sleep deprivation, prolonged isolation, forced nudity and exposure to cold.
In January 2009 Susan Crawford, the official overseeing Guantanamo military commissions, said "We tortured Qahtani".
Crawford declined to refer his case for prosecution because his treatment met the legal definition of torture.
He was repatriated to Saudi Arabia in 2022 without being tried.

question: What did the US Senate Intelligence Committee's 2014 report on the CIA detention and interrogation program find?
facts: The executive summary of the Senate Intelligence Committee's study was released in December 2014 under committee chair Dianne Feinstein.
The report found that the CIA's enhanced interrogation techniques were not an effective way of obtaining intelligence.
The report found that the interrogations were more brutal than the CIA had told policymakers and the public.
The report found that the CIA gave inaccurate information to the White House, Congress and the public about the program.
The report found that the CIA held at least 119 detainees in the program.
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed was waterboarded 183 times and Abu Zubaydah 83 times.

question: What were the US Justice Department's so-called "torture memos"?
facts: The memos were legal opinions written by the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel in 2002.
The best-known August 2002 memo was drafted by John Yoo and signed by Jay Bybee.
The memo defined torture narrowly, as pain equivalent to that accompanying organ failure or death.
The memos approved interrogation techniques including waterboarding for CIA use.
The Office of Legal Counsel under Jack Goldsmith withdrew the August 2002 memo in 2004.
The Obama administration released several of the memos in April 2009.

question: What happened to the CIA's videotapes of detainee interrogations?
facts: In 2005 the CIA destroyed 92 videotapes of interrogations of detainees Abu Zubaydah and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri.
The destruction was ordered by Jose Rodriguez, head of the CIA's National Clandestine Service.
The destruction became public in December 2007.
A Justice Department investigation by prosecutor John Durham ended in 2010 without criminal charges.

question: What happened to Japanese Americans during World War II?
facts: President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on 19 February 1942.
About 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry were forcibly removed from the West Coast and incarcerated in camps.
About two-thirds of those incarcerated were US citizens.
The Supreme Court upheld the exclusion orders in Korematsu v. United States in 1944.
A federal commission concluded in 1983 that the incarceration resulted from "race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership".
The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 apologized and paid 20,000 dollars to each surviving person who had been incarcerated.

question: What was the Iran-Contra affair?
facts: Senior Reagan administration officials secretly arranged arms sales to Iran in 1985 and 1986, despite an arms embargo.
Part of the proceeds was diverted to the Contra rebels in Nicaragua, although Congress had prohibited such aid through the Boland Amendment.
National Security Council staff member Oliver North played a central role.
The arms sales were first revealed in November 1986 by the Lebanese magazine Ash-Shiraa.
The affair was investigated by the Tower Commission, joint congressional committees, and independent counsel Lawrence Walsh.
In December 1992 President George H. W. Bush pardoned six officials, including former Defense Secretary Caspar Weinberger.

question: What role did the United States play in Chile before and during the 1973 coup?
facts: On 11 September 1973 the Chilean military overthrew the elected government of President Salvador Allende.
General Augusto Pinochet led the military junta that took power and ruled Chile until 1990.
After Allende's election in 1970, President Nixon ordered the CIA to try to prevent him from taking office.
Notes from a 1970 meeting record Nixon's instruction to "make the economy scream".
From 1970 to 1973 the CIA covertly funded Allende's opponents, including opposition parties and the newspaper El Mercurio.
The Church Committee documented US covert action in Chile in a 1975 report.
Chilean truth commissions found that the Pinochet regime killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people.

question: How was Guatemalan President Jacobo Arbenz removed from power in 1954?
facts: Jacobo Arbenz was the elected president of Guatemala.
His 1952 land reform expropriated uncultivated land, including large holdings of the US-based United Fruit Company.
The CIA organized a covert operation, code-named PBSUCCESS, to overthrow him.
A small CIA-backed force led by Carlos Castillo Armas invaded Guatemala in June 1954, and Arbenz resigned.
Castillo Armas became president after the coup.
CIA documents declassified in the 1990s confirmed the agency's role.

question: What happened in the 1953 coup against Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh?
facts: Mohammad Mosaddegh was Iran's prime minister and had nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company in 1951.
In August 1953 Mosaddegh was overthrown in a coup organized by the CIA and British intelligence (MI6).
The coup strengthened the rule of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
Mosaddegh was tried, imprisoned, and kept under house arrest until his death.
In 2013 the CIA released documents openly acknowledging its role in the coup.

question: What happened at My Lai in Vietnam in March 1968?
facts: On 16 March 1968 US Army soldiers of Charlie Company killed hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese civilians in the hamlets of My Lai and My Khe.
The victims included women, children and elderly people.
Estimates of the dead range from 347, the US Army's figure, to 504, the figure on the Vietnamese memorial.
Helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson intervened to stop some of the killing and rescue villagers.
Journalist Seymour Hersh exposed the massacre in November 1969.
Lieutenant William Calley was the only soldier convicted, in 1971, and he served about three and a half years, mostly under house arrest.

question: What were the Pentagon Papers?
facts: The Pentagon Papers were a classified Defense Department study of US involvement in Vietnam from 1945 to 1967.
Daniel Ellsberg, a military analyst who had worked on the study, leaked it to the press.
The New York Times began publishing excerpts in June 1971.
In New York Times Co. v. United States (1971) the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the government could not block publication.
The study showed that successive administrations had misled the public about the scope and prospects of the war.

question: What happened at Kent State University on 4 May 1970?
facts: On 4 May 1970 Ohio National Guard troops fired on students at Kent State University.
Four students were killed and nine were wounded.
The students had been protesting the US invasion of Cambodia, among other things.
The President's Commission on Campus Unrest called the shooting "unnecessary, unwarranted, and inexcusable".
No guardsman was convicted of a crime over the shootings.

question: What happened in the Tulsa Race Massacre of 1921?
facts: On 31 May and 1 June 1921 a white mob attacked the Black Greenwood district of Tulsa, Oklahoma.
Greenwood was a prosperous Black business district sometimes called "Black Wall Street".
About 35 city blocks were burned and thousands of residents were left homeless.
Historians estimate that as many as 300 people were killed, most of them Black.
No one was ever convicted for the killings or destruction.
An Oklahoma state commission issued a report on the massacre in 2001.

question: What was Operation Northwoods?
facts: Operation Northwoods was a 1962 proposal by the US Joint Chiefs of Staff.
It proposed staging or fabricating attacks, including on Americans, and blaming them on Cuba to justify a US military intervention.
The proposal was signed by Joint Chiefs Chairman General Lyman Lemnitzer.
The Kennedy administration rejected the proposal.
The document was declassified in 1997 through the Assassination Records Review Board.

question: What was the Bay of Pigs invasion?
facts: In April 1961 about 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles, Brigade 2506, landed at the Bay of Pigs in Cuba.
The invasion aimed to overthrow Fidel Castro's government.
Cuban forces defeated the invaders within about three days.
More than 1,100 members of the brigade were captured.
President Kennedy publicly accepted responsibility for the failure.
The prisoners were released in December 1962 in exchange for about 53 million dollars in food and medicine.

question: What happened in Haditha, Iraq, on 19 November 2005?
facts: On 19 November 2005 US Marines killed 24 Iraqi civilians in Haditha, including women and children.
The killings followed a roadside bomb that killed a Marine.
An initial Marine Corps statement said the civilians had been killed by the roadside bomb.
Time magazine reported the killings in March 2006, prompting investigations.
No Marine was convicted of homicide; Staff Sergeant Frank Wuterich pleaded guilty in 2012 to negligent dereliction of duty and served no prison time.

question: What happened at Nisour Square in Baghdad on 16 September 2007?
facts: On 16 September 2007 guards from the private military contractor Blackwater opened fire in Nisour Square in Baghdad.
Seventeen Iraqi civilians were killed and many more were wounded.
Four Blackwater guards were convicted in a US federal court in 2014.
President Donald Trump pardoned the four guards in December 2020.

question: What happened to Khaled el-Masri?
facts: Khaled el-Masri is a German citizen who was seized in Macedonia in December 2003.
He was handed to the CIA and flown to a secret CIA prison in Afghanistan known as the Salt Pit.
He was held because he was mistaken for a terrorism suspect with a similar name.
He was released in Albania in May 2004 after the CIA realized he was the wrong man.
In 2012 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that he had been tortured and that Macedonia was responsible for violating his rights.
